newsitem.title: USA: Report slams Gingrich, asks rebuke, $300,000 costs.
newsitem.headline: Report slams Gingrich, asks rebuke, $300,000 costs.

text.p: The House ethics committee on Friday issued a scathing report on House Speaker Newt Gingrich, urging a reprimand and a $300,000 penalty to help pay for a two-year inquiry into his admitted ethics breaches.

The report, written for a bipartisan investigative ethics subcommitee by special counsel James Cole, was presented at a hearing of the committee which was to vote on sending it to the full House of Representatives later Friday. The 435-member House is expected to vote on his punishment on Tuesday.

The report said Gingrich agreed a $300,000 penalty was appropriate -- one outcome of bargaining between his lawyers and committee counsel on a settlement to the fierce partisan struggle that has overshadowed all else in the new Congress.

If the committee and House approve the penalty, Gingrich would be the first sitting speaker to be formally reprimanded. The speaker is the third highest elected official of the United States after the president and vice president.
Ethics Chairwoman Nancy Johnson, a Connecticut Republican, described the recommended penalty as "tough and unprecedented compared to past (ethics) cases."
She said the committee believed that the punishment was necessary because the speaker "must be held to the highest ethical standards."
The penalty's severity is exceeded only by expulsion and censure, and the report said the subcommittee felt his offences "fell somewhere in between" reprimand and censure.
Reprimand would allow Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, to remain as speaker but censure might have forced him out.
Gingrich admitted on December 21 that he had provided to ethics investigators "in my name and over my signature, inaccurate, incomplete and unreliable statements."
He also acknowledged he had failed to seek legal advice on whether his use of tax-exempt charitable funds for a college course he taught would violate tax laws.
Gingrich said that he had not intended to mislead the committee but the report took issue with that claim.

It said Gingrich provided false information in letters that said his motivation for teaching the college course was not political and that his political action committee, known as GOPAC, had no involvement.
"In his testimony Gingrich admitted these statements were not true," the report said. "The goal of the letters was to have the complaints dismissed."

"Only Mr Gingrich had personal knowledge of the facts ... Either Mr Gingrich's conduct in regard to the use of (tax-exempt) organisations and the letters submitted to the committee was intentional or it was reckless."
"In addition," the report said, "the violation does not represent only a single instance of reckless conduct."
"Rather, over a number of years and in a number of situations, Mr Gingrich showed a disregard and lack of respect for the standards of conduct that applied to his activities."
The report also said Gingrich broke an agreement with the subcommittee not to make statements about the case following his December 21 admission of ethics violations.

"Both the subcommittee and Mr Gingrich agreed that no public comment should be made about this matter while it is still pending. This includes having surrogates sent out to comment on the matter and attempts to mischaracterize it," the report said.

That agreement has come to the fore in recent days because of publication of a tape of an eavesdropped phone conversation on that date between the speaker and his Republican allies about how to deal with the political fallout from the charges.
A transcript of the phone conversation was leaked to the press and has become the subject of a federal investigation into possible wiretap violations.
Cole summarized the report at the hearing, after which Gingrich lawyer Randolph Evans said: "We do recognise and the speaker recognises how serious the situation is."
But, looking towards Cole, he said: "I disagree with some of the conclusions and analyses."
As the committee neared its climactic vote, Gingrich made an inspirational speech to the Republican National Committee in which he made only one oblique mention of his troubles.
"I don't worry too much about each day's headlines," he said. He declined to answer reporters' questions.
